name: Egypt
summary_text: Egypt is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented study on the treatment of queer foreigners by Egyptian authorities ("Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here," Cairo 52, 12 incidents 2018-2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws (six months + fine for "violation of social and family values") to arrest and prosecute — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under the cybercrime law. Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps (BBC Grindr entrapment) and subject arrestees to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The Ministry of Interior is closing a loophole that allowed limited legal gender recognition. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity in its 2025 Universal Periodic Review. The authorities' approach is described as "not only to criminalize LGBTQ+ identities but also to erase them from society and public life." Egypt has no death penalty for same-sex (unlike Uganda/Nigeria's death penalties), no documented trans-specific tourist killing, and the statutory penalty is six months + fine (not 14 years or life) — but the systematic police entrapment, foreigner-targeting, coerced anal exams, and healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.

sources.title: Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here: A Study on the Treatment of Queer Foreigners by the Egyptian Authorities | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 report 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (Nov 2023) on Egypt's treatment of queer foreigners: analysis of immigration law and 12 incidents (2018-2022). The Ministry of Interior has broad powers to deport or deny entry to anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', interpreted to allow denial of entry and deportation of people perceived as queer; transgender and gender-nonconforming people are most vulnerable to being denied entry.

sources.title: Egypt’s Economic Courts: Homosexuality is Explicitly Criminalized Under Cybercrime Law | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 (Jan 2024): Egypt's Economic Courts (Alexandria) ruled in multiple cases that Article 25 of the Cybercrime Law explicitly criminalises homosexuality (minimum six months' imprisonment plus fines) - a shift from de facto to explicit criminalisation, interpreted alongside 'debauchery' charges under the 1961 Anti-Sex Work Law.

sources.title: Egypt Moves to Close a Loophole Allowing Transgender Individuals Access to Legal Gender Recognition | Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute
sources.claim_summary: Cairo 52 (Dec 2024): the Interior Ministry issued a directive to civil registries closing the loophole that had allowed some trans people legal gender recognition via Civil Status Law record-correction committees - intensifying difficulties for trans people who already face a prohibition on gender-affirming healthcare and active criminalisation.

sources.title: How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps
sources.claim_summary: BBC investigation (Jan 2023): how Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps - undercover officers pose online, initiate text conversations, and in some cases allegedly fabricate evidence; the 'debauchery' law (sex-work law) is used to criminalise LGBT people; around half a million British tourists visit Egypt annually and the UK trains Egyptian police via the UN.

Bedayaa Organisation FAQ on the LGBTIQ situation in Egypt: increasing arrests of gay and trans people, coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye to violations, no anti-discrimination law; covers arrests, detention conditions, and the situation of trans persons.

Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, 'The Trap: Punishing Sexual Difference in Egypt' (2017): documents the police's public-morality units tracking LGBTQ people - three patterns: entrapment (especially of trans women) via fake dating-app accounts; deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without upheld charges; and manufactured media 'scandals' (2014 bathhouse raid, 'gay wedding' case).

sources.title: Egypt | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): no explicit criminalisation but vague public-morality and 'debauchery' laws used for arrests and prison sentences; dating apps (e.g. Grindr) used for entrapment, with condoms or cash used as evidence of 'habitual debauchery'; the 2018 cybercrime law penalises online content 'threatening family values'; no SOGISC discrimination protection; no legal gender recognition and no functioning pathway to gender-affirming healthcare.

sources.title: Egypt’s Fourth Cycle UPR: The Right to Health for Transgender and Intersex Individuals - The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy
sources.claim_summary: TIMEP/Cairo 52 alternate UPR report (Jan 2025) on Egypt's 4th cycle: discriminatory laws, policies and practices prevent transgender and intersex individuals from enjoying the right to health.

sources.title: In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct | HRW
sources.claim_summary: HRW report 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (Feb 2004): landmark report documenting the Egyptian crackdown - the Queen Boat trial, torture of defendants ('Every place we were held, somebody beat us'), the use of 'debauchery' charges, and the assault on justice through the criminal system.
